# Biopython

Exercise 15.1 gave you 45 minutes to write a FASTA parser with no library.
Yours had to glue wrapped lines back together, read past a blank line sitting
inside a record, drop a trailing `*`, and cut each identifier at the first
space. Code that reads FASTA already exists, and it's free. So should you have
written yours?

## A library is code somebody else already debugged

A [library]{.term def="Code somebody else wrote and published for other people
to call. You install it once, import it by name, then use the names inside
it."} is code somebody else wrote and left somewhere your code can reach. You
install it once, you import it, then you call names out of it the same way you
call `translate` out of your own notebook.

Biopython is the one this book installs. It reads three of the five formats
from Chapter 15, it knows the genetic code you loaded into `codon_table` in
Chapter 13, and Chapter 18 is built on it. Colab already carries every other
library this book uses, so this is the only install anywhere in it.

Here's the trade, and it's the whole chapter. You give up knowing exactly what
happens between the file and the answer. You get back every edge case the
people who wrote it have already hit, including the ones nobody has told you
about yet.

## The one install in this book

Every other cell in this book runs on a Colab machine exactly as Google hands
it to you. One line doesn't, and here it is.

``` {.python}
!pip install biopython
```

The exclamation mark says the line isn't Python. Everything after it goes to
the machine underneath your notebook, and `pip` is the program on that machine
that fetches libraries and puts them where Python looks. The download lands on
Google's computer rather than on yours, so it costs you no data and it installs
nothing you'll ever have to remove.

You'll run that line again tomorrow. Colab hands you a fresh machine each
session. Chapter 4 covered what that means: the machine you had last night was
thrown away with everything on it, and this library went with it. So the
install goes at the top of any notebook that needs it, and you run it again
every session. That's the system working, and expecting it is the difference
between a shrug and a lost evening.

`pip` prints a run of lines while it works. None of them is the check. I
haven't reprinted them here, because they name a version and a set of
dependencies that shift between sessions. A copy printed on this page would be
wrong before you read it. Here's the check instead, and it's one cell you can
run any time you're unsure:

```{python}
import Bio

print(Bio.__version__)
```

::: {.check}
A version number prints. The number above came off the machine this page was
built on, and yours can be higher without anything being wrong. What matters is
that a number appears at all instead of red text. If you get
`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'Bio'`, the install cell hasn't run in
this session, and the end of this chapter has the fix.
:::

Colab's own set of preinstalled libraries shifts over time, so one evening
`import Bio` may work before you've installed anything.

::: {.asof}
Checked against Colab on 2 August 2026. Run the install line even when the
import already works. It costs seconds, and it's the difference between a
notebook that runs for you and a notebook that runs for anybody you send it to.
:::

## Walkthrough: reading the file you parsed by hand

`SeqIO` is the part of Biopython that reads and writes sequence files.
`SeqIO.parse` takes a path and the name of a format, and it hands back the
records one at a time.

Before you run the next cell, write down the four lengths you expect. You
measured them yourself in Chapter 15 and the answers were 480, 420, 480 and
180.

```{python}
from Bio import SeqIO

for record in SeqIO.parse("data/sequences/messy.fasta", "fasta"):
    print(record.id, len(record.seq))
```

Three lines, against everything Exercise 15.1 made you write. Three of the four
lengths match what you got by hand, and the fourth doesn't.

Take the matches first. 480 means the wrapped record got glued back together.
420 means the record written on one unbroken line came through whole. Two
wrapping styles inside a single file are no trouble at all. The second 480
means the blank line inside the mouse record didn't end the record. Look at the
identifiers as well, because every one of them arrived cut at the first space.
So `SeqIO` absorbed three of the four defects you found the hard way, and you
never asked it to.

Now the 181. The trailing `*` is still there, and the library kept it on
purpose. In a protein FASTA file, `*` is a legal character. It marks the stop
codon, and your own `translate` from Chapter 14 put one at the end of the
protein it handed you. Nothing tells `SeqIO` whether this file holds DNA or
protein, and it doesn't guess. A parser that quietly deleted `*` would corrupt
every protein file it ever touched, so Biopython leaves the character alone.
You still decide what it means in your own file.

::: {.trap}
`record.id` is everything from the `>` up to the first space, so the species
sits in the part that `record.id` leaves out. Two of the four identifiers in
`messy.fasta` are `NM_007294.4` and `NM_007294.4_translated`, and they stay
apart only because the second one carries an underscore where a space would
have been. Put a space there and both records answer to `NM_007294.4`. Key a
dictionary of your own on `record.id` and the second record lands silently on
top of the first. You'd have three records where you counted four.
:::

Biopython has a shortcut for exactly that job. `SeqIO.to_dict` builds the
dictionary keyed on `record.id`, and it refuses to build one at all when two
ids collide. A dictionary you assemble yourself in a loop refuses nothing.

## What one record hands you

`SeqIO.parse` doesn't give you a list. It gives you one pass over the file, and
the pass runs out at the end of the file. That's how Biopython can open a file
far bigger than the memory your notebook has, and it's why the next cell
surprises people.

```{python}
records = SeqIO.parse("data/sequences/messy.fasta", "fasta")

print(len(list(records)))
print(len(list(records)))
```

Four, then zero, out of the same variable and the same call. The first `list()`
used the pass up, and there's nothing behind it for the second one to read.

::: {.trap}
Nothing errored on that second line and nothing warned you. Loop over the same
`SeqIO.parse` call twice and your second loop body never runs, so a count comes
out as zero and a search finds nothing. The fix is to spend the pass once and
keep what came back.
:::

Wrap the call in `list()` and you have an ordinary Python list you can walk as
many times as you like. Same name, and this time it holds four records instead
of a promise to find four records.

```{python}
records = list(SeqIO.parse("data/sequences/messy.fasta", "fasta"))
first = records[0]

print(len(records))
print(first.id)
print(first.description)
print(type(first.seq))
```

One item out of that list is a
[SeqRecord]{.term def="Biopython's object for one sequence record: an id, a
description, and the sequence itself."}. Three parts of it matter here.
The `.id` attribute holds the identifier, cut at the first space. The
`.description` attribute holds everything after the `>`, cut at nothing. The
`.seq` attribute holds the sequence. Look at the last line of that output,
because it says the sequence isn't a string.

### The format name is the only thing that changes

Chapter 15 walked you through five formats. `SeqIO` reads three of them, and
moving from one to another means editing one string.

| The file holds | You pass |
|---|---|
| FASTA | `"fasta"` |
| FASTQ | `"fastq"` |
| GenBank | `"genbank"` |

Same loop, same `record.id`, same `len(record.seq)`. What changes is how much
each record carries, because a FASTQ record brings its quality string along and
a GenBank record brings the whole annotation block. The other two formats from
Chapter 15 aren't here on purpose. BED and VCF hold coordinates rather than
sequence, so nothing in `SeqIO` reads them. Both are tables, and Chapter 20 is
where this book opens tables.

That second argument is a claim you're making about the file, and nothing
checks it against the file's contents until something goes wrong. The If it
breaks section at the end of this chapter has the error you get when the claim
is false.

## A Seq is a string that knows what it's made of

`first.seq` is a [Seq]{.term def="Biopython's sequence object. It slices and
counts like a string, and it also knows how to complement and translate
itself."}, which behaves like a string everywhere you already know how to use
one. `len()` works on it. Slicing works. `.count("G")` works. It also carries
methods that a plain string has no business carrying.

Here's the human *BRCA1* coding sequence again, sliced out of the same file
Chapter 14 used, at the same two numbers.

```{python}
human = None
for record in SeqIO.parse("data/sequences/brca1_five_species.fasta", "fasta"):
    if record.id.startswith("human"):
        human = record

coding = human.seq[113:5705]

print(len(coding))
print(coding.translate()[:20])
print(coding.reverse_complement()[:20])
```

That's the same 5,592 bases under the same name as before, held as a Seq rather
than as a string. The call to `.translate()` does in one line what your
`translate` function does with a loop and a dictionary. And
`.reverse_complement()` does what your `pairing` dictionary and its backwards
loop did.

<!-- nlr-allow: 1864 -->

::: {.check}
The first twenty residues read `MDLSALRVEEVQNVINAMQK`, which is what Chapter
14's `translate` printed off the identical slice. Don't take the rest of it
from me. If that function is still in your notebook, run
`translate(str(coding)) == str(coding.translate())` and Python answers `True`:
the two agree over all 1,864 characters, ending on the `*` where the stop codon
sits. Print `other_strand[:20]` from the same notebook and you get
`TCAGTAGTGGCTGTGGGGGA`, which is the twenty letters `.reverse_complement()`
just handed you. Two routes to one answer is the strongest evidence you can get
with nobody around to ask.
:::

## What you gave up for that

You gave up being able to look. When your own parser did something strange you
put a `print` in the middle of the loop and watched. You can't do that inside
`SeqIO.parse`. When a library surprises you, you're reading its documentation
rather than watching its behavior.

What you bought is harder to see, because nothing prints when a bug doesn't
happen. Three of your four defects were handled in this chapter without a line
of code from you. The mixed wrapping, the blank line and the spaces in the
headers cost you real minutes in Chapter 15 and cost you nothing here.

So use the library, and keep the check. That 181 is the whole argument. The
library and your expectation disagreed and nothing errored. You could tell
which number answered your question for one reason: you'd written four of them
down before you ran the cell.

Which is also why Chapter 15 came first. You can read that 181 and name the
exact defect it is, in a file you've already taken apart by hand. Somebody who
started here would see a number and write it down.

means you walked the same `SeqIO.parse` call more than once. Last, look at the
two identifiers that share an accession and write down what your code would do
if the underscore in the second one were a space.

## If it breaks

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'Bio'"}
Python is talking, and it went looking for the library in the folders where it
keeps libraries. The install cell hasn't run in this session, which happens
every time the runtime restarts. Run `!pip install biopython` again, then run
your import again. Nothing is wrong with your machine or with the library.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: Duplicate key 'NM_007294.4'"}
Biopython is talking. `SeqIO.to_dict` keys its dictionary on `record.id`, and
two of your headers agree up to their first space. This is the collision the
Trap box above described, except that `to_dict` refuses out loud rather than
overwriting. Key on `record.description` instead, or fix the headers in the
file.
:::

::: {.errfix err="ValueError: Records in Fastq files should start with '@' character"}
Biopython is talking, and it's reporting the first thing that didn't match. You
passed `"fastq"` as the format name for a file that holds FASTA, so it went
looking for the `@` that starts a FASTQ record and found `>`. The format name
is a claim you're making about the file, and nothing checks it for you.
:::

::: {.errfix err="AttributeError: 'SeqRecord' object has no attribute 'sequence'"}
Python is talking, and it's quoting back the name you typed rather than the one
that exists. The attribute is `.seq`. Read the quoted word letter by letter
against what you meant to write.
:::
:::
